newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Stronger crown theme of Swedish company results.
newsitem.headline: Stronger crown theme of Swedish company results.

text.p: Sweden's first-half corporate reporting season saw banks booming, forestries falling and flagship exporters suffering from a stronger crown.
A five percent appreciation in the Swedish currency against the all-important German mark over the first six months of the year took its toll on virtually all of Sweden's manufacturing industry.
Blue chips such as Ericsson, Volvo and Astra, which together account for around a third of the total value of the Swedish market, were no exception.
Telecoms group Ericsson took a 500 million Swedish crown ($75.43 million) currency hit in the first half, and said the profit drain for the year was likely to be around a billion crowns.
But Ericsson's first-half pre-tax earnings of 4.22 billion crowns still came in higher than the market expected, and a 29 percent increase in order intake cheered analysts further.
Volvo's profits actually benefited from the stronger crown to the tune of 200 million crowns at operating level as currency hedging contracts paid off over the first half of the year.
Even so, a firmer crown took its toll on income from foreign sales, and Volvo's pre-tax profit fell 28 percent to 3.86 billion crowns from 5.33 billion in the first half of 1995.

Drugs giant Astra, which at 172 billion crowns has by far the largest market capitalisation of any company listed in Stockholm, said the crown reduced profits by around 600 million crowns in the first half.
This was enough to drag pre-tax earnings of 6.76 billion crowns below market consensus estimates of almost seven billion, but analysts said Astra's growth and margins were not at risk.
While most sectors reported higher earnings for the period, Sweden's forest industry was hit hard by falling product prices and a generally lacklustre market.

Stora's first half profits tumbled to 1.61 billion crowns, 60 percent down on the corresponding period in 1995. The stronger crown was once again partly to blame, but Stora said a weak European economy and stock run-downs by customers were behind a sharp fall in sales.
Sweden's other three forestry majors AssiDoman, SCA and MoDo all reported profit falls of between 36 and 43 percent, and total sector profits were more than halved on the same period last year.

On a more positive note, Sweden's banks finally saw an end to the credit loss spiral of the early part of the decade, and a bullish stock market and falling interest rates helped bolster profits from trading operations.

Handelsbanken's profits climbed 17 percent to 3.00 billion crowns and Nordbanken's profits were up 19 percent to 3.80 billion, while S-E-Banken's earnings of 2.72 billion crowns bore no relation at all to the first half of 1995 when currency speculation wiped out earnings entirely.
On an out-and-out bottom-line comparison, Wallenberg group investment arm Investor was Stockholm's top performing company in the first half.

Pre-tax profits of a massive 11.61 billion crowns were almost entirely due to the sale of truckmaker Scania, although a 12.4 billion crown capital gain on the share sale was partly offset by a 2.48 billion crown cash injection into the Saab Automobile group.
Despite some dramatic percentage movements in earnings, market analysts had accurately predicted crown effects and one-off gains, and there were few surprises among the headline interim reports.
The Stockholm all-share index rose steadily throughout the period for a five percent aggregate gain in August.
